newsitem.title: USA: NY precious metals end up on fund shortcovering.
newsitem.headline: NY precious metals end up on fund shortcovering.

text.p: New York precious metals futures ended solidly higher Monday, with fund shortcovering seen leading the way, despite a bearish fundamental outlook for the complex, analysts said.

"The market remains bearish, but is clearly uncomfortable everytime spot gold dips below $380 and there's been no selling pressure really in the past few days, leaving the funds a little nervous and encouraging some shortcovering," Credit Suisse New York vice president Ian MacDonald said.
"But I don't think gold is really going anywhere until physical demand picks up."

COMEX December gold ended up $1.80 at $383.90 an ounce, after trading up to a session high at $384.00, near the top of the range of the past two weeks, following a dip to a two week intraday low at $381.60 on Friday.
In New York bullion trade, spot gold ended quoted $381.75/382.25 an ounce, against the London afternoon fix at $381.00 and the New York close Friday at $380.10-380.50.
The key $380 support level has held since April 1995, apart from a brief intra-week dip to $376.90, in early October, analysts noted.
COMEX December silver ended up 4.0 cents at $4.937 an ounce, after seeing a session high at $4.955.

Technical analysts noted the momentum of the downtrend of the past six week's has clearly waned, with standard oscillators, such as a nine-day relative strength indicator (RSI) showing some divergence from the price downtrend.
COMEX warehouse stocks of gold and silver have been falling steadily in recent weeks also, with silver stocks seeing 10 year lows last week.
"This silver is being exported to Asia via Europe," Merrill Lynch analyst Ted Arnold said.
"Low western prices have undoutedly encouraged Indian demand in particular and Asian demand in general, but it would be wrong to say that all of this silver is actually being consumed," he said.

"The bulls note that 1996 will see the sixth consecutive year of supply deficits and argue this must point to higher prices, but the bears argue that silver stocks in vaults and throughout the vast supply line are more than sufficient to cover current shortfalls."
In addition, Japanese demand for gold remains weak, with gold trading in Tokyo at a discount to European prices, analysts noted.
NYMEX January platinum ended up 10 cents at $388.30, while NYMEX December palladium closed up $1.15 at $118.50 an ounce.
--Clive Mckeef, New York Commodities 212-859-1641; email: clive.mckeef@reuters.com
